citations.evidenceText:
Why Deep RL?
•  The use of a Q-table is effective for simple problems with limited
   dimensions, but it faces several critical limitations as environments
   increase in complexity.
•  The primary limits of the Q-table approach include:
➢Impracticality in Complex Environments:
   – Tabular methods become impractical when an environment
       has billions of potential states and hundreds of actions for
      each state (for example image-based environments).
➢Lack of Generalization:
   – One of the most significant drawbacks is that Q-tables
       cannot generalize to unseen inputs.
   –  In a table, each cell is independent; if an agent hasn't
        visited a specific state-action pair, its value remains at
          its initial setting (often 0), even if the agent has learned
      about a nearly identical state.

citations.evidenceText:
The Two Networks in DQN
•  DQN constructs its own target (or target value 𝑦) using the Bellman equation, and
    trains the network to match it.
•    If we use the same network 𝜃 for both prediction and generating the target, this will
   make training unstable and prone to oscillation or divergence as we are chasing the
   moving target (every time you update 𝜃 to reduce the loss, the target value itself shifts
    too).
                  Target Network (parameters 𝜙)
 •  This is a frozen (lagged) copy of the main network. It does not
   get updated by gradient descent directly.
 •   Its only job is to compute the target value used in the loss:
           𝑦= 𝑟+ 𝛾max 𝑄(𝑠′, 𝑎′; 𝜙)
                                     𝑎′
 •  Every 𝐹 steps (e.g., every 1,000–10,000 steps), it's refreshed by
   copying the main network's weights: 𝜙←𝜃 (a "replacement
   update") , or 𝜙←𝛽𝜙+ 1 −𝛽𝜃 (a "Polyak/soft update").

Learnable Functions in Deep RL

•  An agent can use a neural network to represent (approximate) any of the
   following:
   – Policy 𝝅𝜽(𝒔): maps a state directly to an action (or action probabilities).
   – Value function 𝑽𝜽(𝒔) or 𝑸𝜽(𝒔, 𝒂): estimates expected future reward.
   – Model 𝑷𝜽(𝒔′ ∣𝒔, 𝒂): predicts the environment's next state and reward
       (used in model-based RL).

•  Each network is "parameterized" by its weights 𝜃.
•  Which function(s) an algorithm learns
   determines what family of Deep RL algorithm
     it belongs to.

concepts.title: Deep RL definition
concepts.description: The diagram combines learning decisions through reward feedback with deep representations or function approximation.

concepts.title: Agent–environment loop
concepts.description: The agent acts on the environment and receives observations and reward after the transition.

concepts.title: Q-learning numerical update
concepts.description: The update moves one fifth of the way from 2 to the target 5.5.

concepts.title: Learning rate versus discount
concepts.description: Learning rate controls an update step; discount controls the contribution of later reward estimates.

concepts.title: Tabular storage burden
concepts.description: Tabular storage scales with the product of represented states, actions and bytes per value.

concepts.title: Generalization versus separate entries
concepts.description: This concerns the specified single-entry update, not every algorithm that uses a table or a model.

concepts.title: Reading a state–action table
concepts.description: Greedy selection uses the largest action value in the current row, not the largest relative increase from a smaller entry.

concepts.title: Product discretization
concepts.description: Cartesian discretization multiplies the per-coordinate bin counts, then multiplies by the number of actions.

concepts.title: Qualifying tabular limits
concepts.description: The useful contrast is scalability and representation quality, not a universal inability of tables to model stochastic motion.

concepts.title: Information lost by coarse state encoding
concepts.description: A compact position representation may omit physically relevant variables; function approximation does not by itself repair missing state information.
concepts.subtopic: Information lost by coarse state encoding

concepts.title: Two Q-network input contracts
concepts.description: Do not silently conflate the scalar state–action architecture with the state-to-action-vector architecture.

concepts.title: Parameter sharing and generalization
concepts.description: Generalization is a capacity to transfer learned structure, not a guarantee that every unseen prediction is correct.

concepts.title: Counting schematic parameters
concepts.description: The parameter count is (3×4+4)+(4×4+4)+(4×4+4)=56.

concepts.title: Reading schematic dimensions
concepts.description: A literal implementation must explicitly choose its input representation; the drawing alone does not establish an undocumented compression.

concepts.title: Interpreting the corridor Q table
concepts.description: Each action is selected by comparing values within the current distance row.

concepts.title: Q values are not probabilities
concepts.description: Raw action-value outputs and action-selection probabilities are different objects.

concepts.title: Unseen-input evaluation
concepts.description: The generalization illustration does not provide weights or an interpolation rule from which to calculate exact unseen outputs.

concepts.title: Matching neural architectures
concepts.description: The matches describe common suitability, not an exclusive rule that forbids other architectures.

concepts.title: Why a recurrent input can help
concepts.description: Temporal context may reduce partial-observation ambiguity, but success still depends on the model and data.
concepts.subtopic: Why a recurrent input can help

concepts.title: Policy, value and model functions
concepts.description: Policies decide, values evaluate and transition models predict state evolution.

concepts.title: Transition model versus reward model
concepts.description: Pθ(s′|s, a) alone denotes a successor-state distribution; it does not by itself specify a reward predictor.

concepts.title: Algorithm-family table
concepts.description: These are introductory associations; categories can overlap, and being named in this table does not make every implementation a deep neural method.

concepts.title: SARSA and DQN comparison
concepts.description: On/off-policy describes the relationship between the behavior data and the evaluated or improved policy, not whether the behavior contains randomness.

concepts.title: State value is not action-indexed
concepts.description: Q(s, a) directly distinguishes actions; V(s) can support action choice with additional model or lookahead information.

concepts.title: DQN scoring and selection
concepts.description: The action-selection mechanism is separate from the Q approximator.

concepts.title: Image-based DQN output
concepts.description: The CNN extracts image features and the output head scores discrete actions in one pass.

concepts.title: Main-network roles
concepts.description: The same main parameters support action scoring and the prediction side of the loss.

concepts.title: Same architecture, different parameters
concepts.description: The networks share a structural form, not necessarily identical parameter values between target updates.

concepts.title: Purpose of the target network
concepts.description: A less rapidly changing target can improve training stability, but no universal convergence guarantee follows.

concepts.title: Hard target update timing
concepts.description: Hard copying replaces the target with the current main parameters at the specified update time.

concepts.title: Soft target update calculation
concepts.description: The update moves the target one tenth of the distance from 2 to 10.

concepts.title: Interpreting the soft-update coefficient
concepts.description: The coefficient β is old-target retention, not the fraction of the main network copied in.

concepts.title: DQN target and TD error
concepts.description: The prediction belongs to the experienced current pair, while the bootstrap maximum comes from the target network at the successor.

concepts.title: Terminal DQN target
concepts.description: The lecture’s unmasked target is applied to nonterminal transitions. The stated true-terminal extension uses only the observed reward.

concepts.title: A fully specified scalar training step
concepts.description: This exact scalar change follows only because the model, loss and learning rate are supplied; it is not asserted for an arbitrary neural network.
concepts.subtopic: A fully specified scalar training step

concepts.title: What an output target does not specify
concepts.description: A target and prediction alone do not specify the neural weight update or its effect on all outputs.
concepts.subtopic: What an output target does not specify

concepts.title: Actual epsilon-greedy probabilities
concepts.description: The exploration branch can select the greedy action, so its total probability is larger than 1−ε.

concepts.title: Exploration branch versus selected action
concepts.description: Behavioral outcome and the branch that produced it are not the same event.

concepts.title: Boltzmann action probabilities
concepts.description: Boltzmann selection exponentiates scaled values and then normalizes them.

concepts.title: Temperature limits
concepts.description: Temperature changes how strongly differences in action values influence sampling.

concepts.title: Stable softmax transformation
concepts.description: Subtracting a common value, often the maximum, preserves the probability ratio while helping numerical evaluation.

concepts.title: Tied maxima at low temperature
concepts.description: A greedy limit need not select a unique action when the values tie.

concepts.title: Classifying obstacle behavior
concepts.description: The classification depends on motion and predictability during the episode, not only on object identity.

concepts.title: Discrete choices and continuous commands
concepts.description: Discrete planning labels and real-valued actuator commands are different action representations.

concepts.title: Finite DQN versus continuous control
concepts.description: Deep state approximation and continuous actuation are distinct issues; the planning/control interface must be specified.

concepts.title: Navigation system components
concepts.description: The system combines learned navigation decisions with a separate closed-loop tracking method.

concepts.title: Physical grid-cell scale
concepts.description: Both representations use the same stated spatial resolution despite different map sizes.

concepts.title: Position cells are not full states
concepts.description: The case-study input includes environmental information beyond a single robot-position index.
concepts.subtopic: Position cells are not full states

concepts.title: Reading the navigation maps
concepts.description: Map colors encode obstacle categories in these figures, not generic value-function semantics.

concepts.title: Episode randomization and motion
concepts.description: Randomized starts vary training situations without necessarily turning every obstacle into a moving one.

concepts.title: Counting the inflated-robot rings
concepts.description: The three groups partition 25 cells as 1+8+16.

concepts.title: Buffer size versus robot radius
concepts.description: The reward buffer is a computational safety region larger than the physical robot base.

concepts.title: What is inflated in the case study?
concepts.description: The figure describes a reward-based region around the robot rather than mechanical enlargement.
concepts.subtopic: What is inflated in the case study?

concepts.title: Environment-dependent penalties
concepts.description: The table specifies two environment-dependent penalty rows, so a single universal penalty list would lose information.

concepts.title: Qualifying the outer-ring penalty
concepts.description: The detailed table qualifies the generic preceding illustration; the question preserves both rather than inventing a global correction.

concepts.title: Explicit reward-accounting example
concepts.description: The aggregation convention is supplied for this calculation; the slide itself only lists component values.

concepts.title: Comparing specified immediate costs
concepts.description: A local cost comparison is not a complete policy decision: collision risk and future return are excluded by the question.

concepts.title: Using the correct environment reward
concepts.description: Correct target construction requires both the appropriate task reward and the specified terminal convention.

concepts.title: Scope of reported navigation results
concepts.description: The lecture reports empirical generalization in particular simulations, not a theorem about all unseen obstacle motion.

concepts.title: Tracking accuracy versus obstacle clearance
concepts.description: The source’s reported gap is retained as an empirical claim; tracking plots alone are not sufficient evidence of obstacle separation.

concepts.title: Sample inefficiency
concepts.description: The source’s millions-of-interactions example motivates the challenge without fixing a universal count.

concepts.title: Behavior–data feedback
concepts.description: Learning decisions and collected experience form a feedback loop; a stable architecture alone does not remove this dependence.

concepts.title: A reward-shaping failure
concepts.description: A shaped signal must be checked against the actual desired task, not merely whether it provides frequent feedback.

concepts.title: Sparse feedback
concepts.description: Sparse rewards can make discovery and credit assignment difficult; they do not make learning logically impossible.

concepts.title: Mapping spatial zones to penalties
concepts.description: The spatial labels and environment-specific table must be read together. This asks for listed components, not an unstated simultaneous-event sum.

concepts.title: What an actor–critic combines
concepts.description: Combined actor–critic methods connect policy learning with value estimation; they need not learn transition dynamics.
